content: EP300, also known as histone acetyltransferase p300 (p300 HAT) or E1A-associated protein p300 (where E1A refers to adenovirus early region 1A), is an enzyme encoded by the EP300 gene in humans. This enzyme functions as a histone acetyltransferase, playing a critical role in regulating gene transcription through chromatin remodeling. It is essential for controlling cell growth and division, promoting cellular differentiation (the process by which cells mature and acquire specialized functions), and inhibiting the development of cancerous tumors. The p300 protein is vital for normal development both before and after birth. The EP300 gene encodes a transcriptional co-activator protein that interacts with the adenovirus E1A protein. EP300 is closely related to another gene, CREB-binding protein (CBP), which is located on human chromosome 16. Function The p300 HAT enzyme regulates transcription by acetylating histones, which facilitates chromatin remodeling. This activity is crucial for processes such as cell proliferation and differentiation. Additionally, p300 mediates cAMP-dependent gene regulation by specifically binding to phosphorylated CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein). The EP300 gene also acts as a co-activator of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1A), thereby contributing to the activation of hypoxia-induced genes, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Mechanism The p300 protein activates transcription by binding to transcription factors and the transcriptional machinery. Due to this role, it is classified as a transcriptional co-activator. The interaction between p300 and transcription factors is mediated by specific domains within the p300 protein, including the nuclear receptor interaction domain (RID), the KIX domain (which interacts with CREB and MYB), the cysteine/histidine-rich regions (TAZ1/CH1 and TAZ2/CH3), and the interferon response binding domain (IBiD). Notably, the KIX, TAZ1, TAZ2, and IBiD domains of p300 tightly bind to the transactivation domains (9aa TADs) of the transcription factor p53. Clinical Significance Mutations in the EP300 gene are responsible for a small percentage of cases of Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome. These mutations result in the loss of one copy of the gene in each cell, reducing the amount of functional p300 protein by half. Some mutations produce a truncated, nonfunctional version of the p300 protein, while others prevent one copy of the gene from producing any protein at all. Although the exact mechanism by which reduced p300 levels lead to the specific features of Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome is not fully understood, it is evident that the loss of one EP300 gene copy disrupts normal development. Chromosomal rearrangements involving chromosome 22, where the EP300 gene is located, have been associated with certain types of cancer, though these occurrences are rare. For example, a translocation between chromosomes 8 and 22 has been identified in some individuals with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a cancer of blood cells. Another translocation, involving chromosomes 11 and 22, has been observed in a small number of individuals who developed AML following chemotherapy for other cancers. These chromosomal changes disrupt the EP300 gene region, contributing to cancer development. Somatic mutations in the EP300 gene, which are acquired during a person’s lifetime and present only in certain cells, have been identified in various cancers. These include cancers of the colon and rectum, stomach, breast, and pancreas. Research suggests that EP300 mutations may also play a role in the development of some prostate cancers and could help predict whether these tumors will grow or metastasize. In cancer cells, EP300 mutations often prevent the production of functional p300 protein. Without p300, cells lose the ability to effectively regulate growth and division, which can lead to the formation of cancerous tumors. Interactions EP300 has been shown to interact with numerous proteins, including: BCL3 BRCA1 CDX2 CEBPB CITED1 CITED2 DDX5 DTX1 EID1 ELK1 ESR1 FEN1 GPS2 HIF1A HNF1A HNRPU ING4 ING5 IRF2 LEF1 MAF MAML1 MEF2C MEF2D MYBL2 Mdm2 MyoD MEF2A NCOA6 NFATC2 NPAS2 p53 PAX6 PCNA PROX1 PTMA PPARA PPARG RORA RELA SMAD1 SMAD2 SMAD7 SNIP1 SS18 STAT3 STAT6 TAL1 TCF3 TFAP2A TGS1 TRERF1 TSG101 THRA TWIST1 YY1 Zif268 These interactions highlight the diverse roles of p300 in cellular processes, including transcriptional regulation, DNA repair, and response to environmental signals.
